answer.label: Not Mahatma Gandhi — an old American adage
answer.authorName: Earliest known use: George Hyde Preston, 1908 (QI unsure if he coined it)
answer.authorDates: First documented 1908 · a Wall Street / folk expression
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Gandhi ever said or wrote this. Quote Investigator traced the earliest strong match to a 1908 short story, “An Inside Tip” by George Hyde Preston in Cosmopolitan, where a stock-market “bear” declares “If you are going to be a bear, be a grizzly!” — and even that may only be recording a pre-existing anonymous adage. The Gandhi tag first surfaced online around 2008.

source.heading: The real trail
source.excerpt: “If you are going to be a bear, be a grizzly!”
source.trailTitle: From folk adage to fake Gandhi
trail: The line is plastered across quote sites as Mahatma Gandhi, but it appears nowhere in his Collected Works, and Quote Investigator found no substantive evidence he ever said or wrote it ↗.

The earliest strong match is a 1908 Cosmopolitan short story, “An Inside Tip” by George Hyde Preston, where a Wall-Street operator declares “If you are going to be a bear, be a grizzly! ↗” — a pun on stock-market “bears.”
The saying recurs in American life for decades — a 1959 Chicago Daily Tribune item and Lady Bird Johnson’s published diary both quote it ↗ — long before anyone tied it to Gandhi.
The Gandhi tag appears to originate with a 2008 Goodreads post that ascribed the line to him without any citation ↗.
source.excerptNote: As spoken by a stock-market “bear” in George Hyde Preston’s 1908 story — the earliest strong match located by Quote Investigator, which notes even this may echo a pre-existing anonymous saying.

source.rightsNote: The earliest documented appearance is George Hyde Preston’s short story “An Inside Tip” in Cosmopolitan (1908) — published in the United States well before 1931, so that text is in the public domain. Quote Investigator is unsure whether Preston coined the expression or was recording a saying that may predate that printing.

author.name: Mahatma Gandhi
author.heading: Why it isn't Gandhi
author.metaLine: 1869–1948 · Indian independence leader & apostle of nonviolence
author.bio: Mohandas Karamchand “Mahatma” Gandhi led India’s independence movement through satyagraha — nonviolent civil resistance. A committed pacifist, his voluminous Collected Works run to roughly 100 volumes, none of which contain this bellicose one-liner. The saying’s aggressive, predator-take-all sentiment runs directly against his philosophy, which is part of why the misattribution is so conspicuous.

misattribution.heading: How Gandhi got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook feel-good misattribution: an aggressive, decades-old American adage retrofitted onto history’s most famous pacifist.

items.why: The line appears nowhere in Gandhi’s writings or speeches; Quote Investigator located no substantive evidence he said or wrote it ↗. Its predator-dominance message is the opposite of his nonviolent philosophy.
The Gandhi ascription traces online to a 2008 Goodreads posting that gave no citation ↗, after which quote aggregators copied it endlessly.

The first strong match is Preston’s Cosmopolitan story “An Inside Tip,” where a stock-market bear says “If you are going to be a bear, be a grizzly! ↗” — and even this may be recording an older anonymous saying.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: it’s an old American adage — a pun on Wall-Street “bears” documented by 1908 ↗ — and there is no evidence Gandhi ever said it.

context.heading: Why the wording gives it away
lead: The saying trades on a stock-market pun: a “bear” bets a price will fall, and to be a “grizzly” is to bet aggressively. That origin fits a 1908 Wall-Street story far better than the writings of a man who preached nonviolence.

The mismatch is exactly what makes the misattribution spread: pinning a swaggering, take-no-prisoners line on Gandhi feels surprising enough to be shareable, and few people stop to check whether he actually said it.
context.pull: An old Wall-Street pun, not the words of a pacifist.
